newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain fears further ETA separatist attacks.
newsitem.headline: Spain fears further ETA separatist attacks.

text.p: Spain's government fears Basque separatist guerrillas will strike again soon after kidnapping and killing a young politician.
"I think they are going to attack soon and make us suffer again," Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja said in an interview published on Sunday in newspaper Diario de Burgos.
"We should not be afraid of the assassins, but we have to know how to fight them. A society cannot be brought to its knees and blackmailed by the anguish of terror."

Basque analysts say a decision by guerrillas of ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) to ignore massive street demonstrations and to coldly assassinate 29-year-old Miguel Angel Blanco two days after kidnapping him suggests the group could launch more attacks.
Spaniards took to the streets in droves -- an estimated six million protested against Blanco's killing.
The assassination, days after police rescued another ETA hostage from 532 days of captivity, unleashed public outrage.
Blanco was shot twice in the head. He died a week ago. In the past week politicians have been scrambling to take advantage of enraged public opinion.
Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar called it a watershed in Spain's response to separatist violence and promised to step up the fight against the guerrilla group.
"The terrorists not only committed a brutal crime...but made an irreparable rupture of ETA and HB (ETA's political wing) with society," Aznar told newspaper El Correo in remarks published on Sunday.
He said the government was seeking legislative reforms to plug loopholes exploited by the guerrillas.
Basque region leaders called on ETA guerrillas on Saturday to follow the example of the Irish Republican Army and declare a truce, saying the time had come to "put a stop to the killing".
An opinion poll published on Sunday showed that nearly 90 percent of Basques wanted the government to begin negotiations with ETA if it unconditionally abandoned violence.
ETA, which has killed some 800 people, started its campaign for an independent Basque state at a time of intense repression in the region under dictator General Francisco Franco.

Although nationalist sentiment still runs high in the region, a substantial majority of Basques say they approve of a tough crackdown on the guerrillas and their supporters, according to the poll in newspaper El Mundo.

Government proposals to outlaw counter-demonstrations and those by masked people were supported by 66 percent and 77 percent of Basques respectively. A move to criminalise the defence of terrorism was backed by 72 percent and 76 percent approved of tougher penalties for vandalism.
Most of the 800 Basques polled by telephone last Wednesday and Thursday said they wanted the government to act quickly rather than waiting for emotions to cool.
